utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Registrar -- not registrar, Usher, could you escort the witness out of the court again, please, for a moment. I'll explain to you --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm told by Madam Vidovic that we are not receiving any interpretation in Serbo-Croat. Are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Are you sure it is on the right channel?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to keep talking until I get an indication from the Serbo-Croat-speaking members. Are you receiving?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not, but I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not you who needs interpretation. It's the accused who needs interpretation. So you're not receiving it as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we still have a problem. No, it's not a problem. In the meantime, I will just explain why I sent the witness out. There may be some questions on identification of the accused, and obviously the next step would have been for me to ask the accused to stand up and declare whether he is receiving interpretation in his own language, which would have identified in the presence of the witness, so I have sent the witness out again. Are you receiving interpretation or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. For a very short well, we were receiving interpretation. But now it's gone again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to think of it, we were offered to work in Courtroom I, which would have entailed a 20-minute delay, and I said no, we can't afford to lose 20 minutes. Is it working now? Are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Oric, I just want to confirm for the time being that you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I'm not receiving any interpretation. I didn't understand a single word being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we still have the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Channel 6, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what channel it should be. I will try again. I will keep on talking, checking whether you are receiving interpretation. But I see that the accused is not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not receiving anything as yet? Nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are receiving interpretation in your own language now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Since we have had this technical problem, Mr. Oric, please, if at any moment, the interpretation -- flow of interpretation is interrupted, or you're not receiving interpretation in any case, please draw my attention immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. No problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Also, good morning to the Defence team. I'm here together with Ms. Patricia Sellers, as well as co-counsel Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. Later on in this session, Mr. Jose Doria will join us as well, as Ms. Patricia Sellers will leave us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned colleagues from the OTP. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just in order to put my mind at rest, I take it, since I haven't seen any signs, that there are no problems with receiving audio and interpretation in the interpretation booths themselves. All right? Okay. So everything seems to be going on fine. I repeat what I said earlier: I sent the witness out because there may be the need for some questions related to identification of the accused, and the last thing I would have wanted to happen is for me to ask the accused to stand up and identify himself in the presence of the witness himself, although obviously we are not going to ask the witness, Do you identify Naser Oric in this courtroom? Because I understand, and we know that that is not the practice in this Tribunal. So let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gligic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. My apologies to you for keeping you waiting outside for a few minutes, but we had one small business to transact, and in addition we had a technical problem with regard to interpretation, which brings me to the first point. I want to make sure that what I am saying in English is being translated to you in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because that is precisely the problem that we had. The interpretation in B/C/S was not arriving. You're testifying under the same solemn declaration that you made two days ago. Madam Sellers, you've got a few minutes, not more than that, to finish your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It will only take a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gligic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Judge Agius just mentioned that you are still under the oath that you took yesterday to tell the truth in your responses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The day before, Madam Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, it's the day before now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- to tell the truth in your responses in questions either to both the Defence and to the Prosecution. Mr. Gligic, do you take that oath seriously?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And have you been truthful in your answers before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And so when you testified the day before yesterday that on one occasion you spoke to Muslim prisoners who told you that they had been ordered by Naser Oric to loot villages, were you telling the Trial Chamber the truth?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you testified to this Trial Chamber that you saw the person that you recognised as Naser Oric present at one of the exchanges, were you telling the Trial Chamber the truth?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Brydensholt has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: It is dealing with the same episode as you have just explained about, namely, when the father and the son, the Muslim father and the son, were being taken by you to be exchanged. What exactly did the father tell you? Try to recall the words he said to you. And what had you said to him beforehand? Could you try to be precise on this point.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time I took them to the exchange, we spoke. They sat next to me. We talked about the war, that no one had really needed this war, us or them, and that no one was to blame. When I said that, the gentleman said that he was also not to blame because he was forced to go and loot; that he had been forced by Mr. Naser Oric and the Srebrenica command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Did he mention that that was an order given directly to him by Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what he said to me: That he had been ordered by the command in Srebrenica, led by Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Now, when the last exchange occurred, there was snow, wasn't there? High snow.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And you explained that you saw Naser Oric on a horse, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And that meant that his guard was standing in the snow, in the high snow, and that he still was sitting on that horse in this high snow, at the top of the hill where you were, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The distance was between 20 and 25 metres. He was on horseback. And around him were his security people, who were armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Brydensholt. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Some of my questions have already been answered, but I still have two or three. Mr. Gligic, when you have been asked why the Muslim people left their villages, their houses and villages, you told us that they did it on their free will. Now, what did you mean with "free will"? Was it their own choice to do this, or had there been some reasons why to leave?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, I think mistrust is what caused that, lack of trust. They saw that only Serbs remained in Skelani, and they were probably afraid because there was already a great deal of mistrust, mutual mistrust between Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Does this mean that they had been forced, or was it more fear of being in danger in the future?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was for fear. They felt that there would be a huge war, and that's why they left their homes. I can only speak about Skelani, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, my second question refers to this Mandzic. You told us about Besim Mandzic. There seems to have been -- to exist also a Nesib Mandzic. Are you aware that there are two persons with the surname of Mandzic but with different first names?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite true. He has a younger brother who was born in 1964, whereas Nesib was born in 1961. I may have got the two of them mixed up at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And the Mandzic you had in mind, I think it was Besim Mandzic, he had been mayor of Srebrenica. At what time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic was mayor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Which one, Besim?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His real name is Nesib. It's me who got the names confused. Nesib Mandzic. I'm not sure what his brother's name is. It might be Besim, but I'm not sure. I only know that the man I'm talking about now was Srebrenica's mayor. I can't specify the exact time period now. It was in 1996, 1997, 1998, thereabouts. The first mayor, the first Muslim mayor in Srebrenica, after everything happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday you spoke about that he was mayor after the war. And what did you mean with "after the war"? Which time did you have in mind when you talk about after the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war ended in Bosnia, when the new authorities were set up in Srebrenica municipality, when Skelani became a municipality, and there was a municipality in Srebrenica too. After a certain time, Serbs were in power in Srebrenica, pursuant to a decision of the High Commission of Wolfgang Petritsch. Mr. Mandzic then became mayor of the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have a last question with regard to this so-called Independent Battalion. Why was it called independent? Independent from what?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I only know that its name was Independent Battalion. I have no idea what that means, but that's what its name was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Was it part of the Territorial Defence, or was it somehow separate from the army and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in August, June, and July, we had the TO, and then the TO became the Independent Battalion. That's what it got to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. Let me take up straight away this Mandzic matter, once it was raised by Judge Eser and you answered in the way you did. In your statement to the Prosecutor, and during your testimony here, you gave details of several contacts with a Mandzic. Yesterday, when you were asked for the name, you repeated that it was Besim; today you are moving from that and accepting that you may have made a mistake. What I want to know from you is whether this Mandzic that you referred to in your statement to the Prosecutor and in your testimony yesterday was the same Mandzic who was mayor in Srebrenica, or whether it was someone else.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same person who was Srebrenica's mayor. He's a neighbour of mine. But, sir, I forget his name. It's been quite a while and I never asked myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not a problem. But yesterday, you did react quite -- in a very explicit way to the question that was put to you by Madam Vidovic, almost angrily, saying that you know better than she does because this guy is your neighbour, and you can't really make a mistake with regard to his name. But forget that. You also mentioned, in the course of your testimony and in your statement, a person called Mandza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is Mandza and Mandzic the same, or is it a different person?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Different persons. So when you say in your statement -- please, could the witness be shown his statement to the Prosecution, or I can read -- I can read out to you. You are describing to the investigator of the Prosecution an exchange, a particular exchange, when five persons were exchanged, the final exchange. And you say: "The same five persons that I had seen on the other occasions met me. However, on this occasion, Naser Oric was there, his security was there. They were all dressed the same as before, and they behaved the same as before. Naser did not move forward or communicate with me at all, but he did talk to Mandzic, who went and talked to him." Was it Mandzic or was it Mandza who was present on that occasion and went to speak to Naser Oric, or to the person who you say was Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, Nesib, whose first name I confused with the other first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Was the person Mandza ever present during any of the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the first occasion, Mandza was in all subsequent exchanges. As far as I know, he hails from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Was there any resemblance between Mandza and the person you describe as Naser Oric? Did they look -- did they resemble each other? Did they look alike?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well that Mr. Mandza had a large moustache and wore a hat, a camouflage hat, on his head. Mr. Oric, when we saw him, had a black beret and a camouflage uniform on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but what I'm saying is the physiognomy, I'm referring to the physiognomy. Did they have the same kind of corporature [sic], did they have the same kind of body? Did they look alike?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mandza was clean-shaven, and Mr. Naser Oric had a beard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But is there any resemblance? Does their face features, for example -- facial features, are they similar?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I didn't really look closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You also mentioned, during your testimony the day before yesterday, that after the two or three occasions that you referred to as having seen the person that you mention as -- you say was Naser Oric, you've had an occasion to see that person several times on videos, you said, and on -- where else? Where else did you see that person that you say is Naser Oric? You saw him in the gym, you saw him in the cafe, you saw him during one of the exchanges. Where else did you see him? You mentioned papers, you mentioned videos, several TV ...

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched a tape where the gentleman explained how they came in from the Bratunac side, towards the Zuti Most area, how the army, or I don't know who, entered the area. I have that videotape, or rather, I can obtain it. That's a tape in which he explains how those people were ambushed and killed. I read a book entitled "The Plight of Kravica," and in that book there are several pictures of the gentleman who posed with the fighters. This is a book that can be bought in Bratunac, in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you shown during your questioning or interviews with the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, were you shown any photos of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean here, in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or in Yugoslavia, when you were interrogated.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in Yugoslavia, not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And here.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, the lady who interviewed me put on the screen a photograph and asked me, "Who is this?" And I said, "Mr. Naser Oric."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What photograph was it? What did it show?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, there were two photographs. In one photograph, he was depicted sitting in the foreground, and in the background were his men. That was in one photograph. And in the other photograph, he was depicted in an orchard with his people, exercising on the horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Did you bring or show to the interrogator from the Office of the Prosecutor, investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, any video or any photos or any press cuttings relating to Naser Oric? Did you bring anything with you, or did you show the Prosecution anything?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV GLIGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I don't think I have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one matter. Since Your Honour referred to part of the 2000 statement of this witness, in which you referred to five persons, I want to be clear for the record, since that may not be exhibited, that obviously the same five persons who referred to at each exchange does not include Naser Oric. It may be obvious from the context. But it's 01007015, for the record. Secondly, just for clarification, it's Hazim Mrki who we say has a striking physical resemblance, not Mandza. That may be useful for the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's all. Mr. Gligic, we have come to an end. On behalf of the Tribunal, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and myself, I would like to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this case against Naser Oric. I know that it wasn't easy, but, in any case, I do thank you for your cooperation. You will be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher, and you will receive all the assistance you require by our staff to facilitate your return back home as soon as possible. On behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise if I wasn't clear enough when expressing all of these details. A lot of time has passed in the meantime, and after all, that was wartime and many emotions emanate from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you, Mr. Gligic, that we are fully aware of that, and we fully sympathise also that living those events is traumatic, and that that kind of trauma people tend to live with for a long number of years. So you have our sympathy and you have our understanding. I can assure you that there were moments when we drew your attention to be more precise, this was because we were doing our duty, and for no other reason. I thank you, Mr. Gligic. You will now be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that closes the first chapter. Now, I am advised, and I need your cooperation a little bit, the technicians need a short interval of time to put in place a new video cassette, yes, and in addition to prepare the courtroom for the protective measures that we have put in place for the next witness. So my suggestion to you is, they don't need more than five minutes, so we have two options: It's a quarter to ten, or twenty to ten. I think we stop for five minutes. Please don't go anywhere far so that we can resume as soon as the courtroom is ready. Usually they even take less than five minutes. So I ask for your cooperation, that's all. All right? Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I have that ... All right. Let's go into private session for a minute or so, please. I want to communicate something to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed, since we have also -- since we have had some problems with the -- technical problems with interpretation this morning, I want to make sure that what I am saying in English is being translated to you in your own language, and that you can hear it -- hear the interpretation properly. Can I have a confirmation of that, to start with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: I can hear the witness very poorly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't blame you. I see that one of the microphones is facing me rather than facing the witness, but I that is on purpose. You have the special microphone; I see, yes. All right. I think I will simplify matters. You can sit down so that you will be near to the microphone. Please do sit down. All right. So you are receiving interpretation in your own language? Could you confirm that to me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Should you want the sound level higher or lower, then it is now, please tell Madam Usher, standing next to you, and she will accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can barely here the witness, and I don't think his microphone is working, because we hear him through other people's microphones, not through his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I thank the English booth for drawing my attention. I have been told that the witness' voice can barely be heard -- can barely be heard, and that they are hearing his voice through the microphones of others, which shouldn't be, actually. Yes, except I see that only my microphone is on. So that shouldn't be happening. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Are the other booths, the B/C/S and French booth, encountering the same problem? I see that the B/C/S is not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French booth is not hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The French booth is not hearing either. So we have -- can I ask you, sir, to speak out somewhat louder and speak into your microphone, the big microphone that you have in front of you, because we seem to have a technical problem. Can you say, "I have heard what you said. I am going to speak a little bit louder." Can you say that into your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard what you said, and I will speak louder.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's fine now, Your Honour. The French booth is okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I see the B/C/S booth is okay as well. So, again, I go back to where I interrupted myself. Should you -- is the sound level in your headphones the correct -- is it correct, or would you like it higher or lower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you know that you have come here to give evidence in this case instituted by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal against Naser Oric. You will be here for quite some time. Your testimony is not going to finish today, and neither tomorrow, I think, so you'll definitely be here until Friday, probably. I hope you have been prepared for that. The next thing I want to tell you is that our Rules require that, before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration, something like an oath - it's actually equivalent to an oath - a solemn declaration something to the effect that during the course of your testimony you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The next of the solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper which I know that usher has already shown you and which she is going to hand to you now. You may remain seated. You can remain seated. Please read out that text aloud so that everyone can hear it, and that would be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. There are a few other things that I need to explain to you now. First of all, before you came here, you asked the Prosecution for some protective measures. The Prosecution asked us, and when I say "us," it's me as the Presiding Judge, my name is Carmel Agius from Malta, Judge Brydensholt from Denmark, and Judge Albin Eser from Germany, the Prosecution asked us on your behalf for protective measures because of certain concerns that you and the Office of the Prosecutor had. I am pleased to confirm to you that we granted these protective measures, and I will explain to you precisely what they are. First of all, the aim of these protective measures is to hide your identity, and we decided to hide your identity because we felt that there were sufficient reasons, the request was justified. How are we hiding your identity? In three ways: First of all, we are hiding your name. Your name will not be mentioned here. And I am appealing to both sides, Prosecution and Defence, to exercise the utmost caution not to address the witness by his name. I know that sometimes mistakes happen, and mistakes are inevitable and that there are remedies, because we are transmitting with a 30-minute delay, I suppose. But please play your utmost attention not to call the witness by his name. So no one will call you by your name. You will be addressed as sir, or Mr. Witness, but not by means of your name. Instead, you have been given a number. And you are Witness C007, a number which I'm sure you have heard before and which will be difficult for you to forget.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard it, but I'm not sure exactly in relation to what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are also hiding your face, and if you look at your monitor, you will soon see how others outside this courtroom will be seeing you. This is precisely how you will look to others: A screen full of cubes, squares, which hide your face from the outside world. The last is voice distortion. I can't show you how others will be hearing what you will be telling us, but I can assure you it will be in such a way that no one can ever get anywhere near identifying your voice. So are you satisfied with these protective measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I also want to make sure that you are feeling comfortable. I don't want you to feel nervous, especially having told you that you will be here for at least three days. You will be asked a series of questions from Mr. Di Fazio, first, who is appearing for the Prosecution in this case, together with others. And after him, you will be asked questions by Mr. Jones, who is one of the lawyers appearing for Naser Oric. In answering these questions, in accordance with the oath that you took a few minutes ago, your duty, your legal and moral duty, is to answer them as truthfully and as fully as possible, and also, to the best of your ability. I know that sometimes remembering things that happened 12 years ago is not easy, but please try to concentrate to give us as accurate an answer as possible each time you are asked a question. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine, Your Honours. Clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the last thing I wanted to tell you is the following: That should, at any moment, you need a rest, or should you not be feeling well and want me to -- want the Trial Chamber, want us, to interrupt, stop the sitting, interrupt it or even stop it, please draw our attention straightaway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually, each session lasts about an hour, an hour and a half, except the last one, which is only about three-quarters of an hour. So they are long sessions. If you need frequent breaks, do let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. I'll do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we can start. One last thing, just one last thing: If you could kindly, when you answer your questions, speak, again, a little bit louder, because I notice that as we go along, you have gone back to speaking very -- at a very low level and a low voice, and I think that creates problems. So try to raise your voice as much as you can without, of course, shouting. The last thing is this: I want to draw your attention that when we are having voice distortion, it is important that when the accused has his microphone switched on, when he is speaking, that all other microphones are switched off, and that includes mine, of course. But please make sure that none of you have got the microphone switched on when the accused is testifying. Last thing, I want to make sure that no one is carrying any mobile phones in this courtroom. That's the last thing I wanted to make sure, all right? So we can start. Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just show you this document, if Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me, in fact, explain it to him. I'm going to ask the usher to show you a piece of paper now on which there is your name and surname written. I just want you to look at that piece of paper, and then I will ask you a very simple question: Does that piece of paper show your name and surname? And you tell me yes or no, that's all. You don't read it. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's got father's name, date of birth on it as well, but I don't think that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay. Usher, could you show it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is accurate. Okay. So that document will be shown now to the Defence, who will see it too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecutor could please just check the father's name, and for the witness too, to check it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you hand it back to the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's misspelled. Two letters have been switched around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mark it. Make the usual --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It I just write on it, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And then you'll show it again to the witness, who will be able to see where the spelling mistake was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again, tell me, please, whether that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen, Witness, we took great pains to hide your identity, and now you mention your father's name yourself. Let's redact it. I will sign it. Let's see the document, please, Madam Usher. This will be given exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P481, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And under seal. P481, and under seal. Yes, you have 12, 13 minutes, Mr. Di Fazio, before we break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours please. I have to go into personal details, so this might be an appropriate moment to go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. We are in open session, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, in early 1992, did you own a hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was it licensed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. I had a weapon permit, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Other than the hunting rifle, did you own or did you have in your possession any other weapons at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've told us that you went to Serbia, and that you returned. Prior to leaving for Serbia with your family, did you do anything with your rifle, your hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. I hid my hunting rifle under a pile of stones and left it there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. In early 1992, were you a member of the JNA or the VRS or any village guard of any type or description whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: No. I only served my mandatory military service with the JNA in 1975 and 1976. Other than that, no one ever called me up to do any service.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've told the Trial Chamber that you returned to your village. Don't mention the name of your home village in the ensuing questions. And can you tell the Trial Chamber why it was that, having taken your family to Serbia, you returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I returned because I had cattle and I needed either to transfer it or to sell it in order to join my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How did you actually get back to your village and your farm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I returned via the Drina River. There was a boat, and I took the boat across the river, and then I travelled via Lijesce to my home place.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: At the time that you returned, did you own cattle, horses -- did you own cattle or horses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, two horses, one cow, and several pigs. I couldn't tell you the exact figure. That's what I had.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened when you returned to your farm and your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: When I returned to my farm from Serbia, they arrested me. There were five of them who did that. The house was all broken down. The couch had been taken outside, and I guess they sat on it. I don't know what they did. Not much time had elapsed before they arrested me. They arrested me right away.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you actually on your farm at the time that you were arrested or picked up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, thinking back, describe to the Trial Chamber how these men who arrested you were dressed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: As far as I remember it now, the two of them wore a uniform, and the rest of them had partial uniforms. There was a total of five of them. And I think that one among them was some kind of a superior to them. And when they harassed me, he would say, "Stop with that, don't do that anymore," and they would listen to him, so I concluded that he was superior.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thanks. You said they had uniform. What sort of uniform, one plain colour or camouflage uniform? Or was it any sort of other uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I couldn't say now exactly what kind of a uniform it was. I remember that it was a camouflage uniform. Now, as to the colour and other factors, I couldn't really say. I was afraid; therefore, I couldn't really observe everything.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. And did they have anything around their head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: As to the colour of the stars and the sickle, I really can't remember what the colours were.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You seem to be referring to something that had stars and a sickle. Think about carefully, and tell the Trial Chamber, if you can remember, any symbols you may have seen, and on what you saw these symbols.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Those were insignia they wore on their foreheads. They had a bandana, a red bandanna, with a star and a sickle. They bore it on their heads.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The sickle was the symbol of a farming implement as used in old communist flags, that sort of sickle. Is that the sort of sickle you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's simplify it. Could the witness be given a piece of paper and a pen, and could he draw it for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the bandanna and the star?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Draw what you saw, particularly the sickle, what has been referred to as a sickle. If you can draw it up, it will help us a lot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was something like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let us see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Show it to Mr. Di Fazio and the Defence, and then put it -- show it to the parties, and then put it on the ELMO, please. Thank you. Put it on the ELMO, please, so the public can see it as well. Witness, let me ask you something: It seems that in the centre of that bandanna, there is something that looks like a big letter C. Is that what you referred to as the sickle, or what was translated to us as the sickle, before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It looks like a sickle, if you ask me. It's not quite there, but it's very much like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it also look, to you, as a big C, like a big letter C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It looked like the moon, young moon, crescent. That's what I mean, like a sickle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That gets us there. And what we see on either side of this crescent that you've just mentioned, we see one, two -- are those what -- the stars you referred to earlier on in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these are the two or three stars that were on the bandanna. I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that into evidence, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it will be tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P483.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be P483. Can you give it back to the witness, please, ask him to put his initials on it, and we will register it and store it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What am I supposed to do with this?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, can you just put your initials on the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that will be P483, and it will be kept under seal. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, I'm sorry for going so slowly and interrupting you every so often, but I think it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honour took me where I was going, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The men that you have described, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed. But I'm not sure if all of them were. I can't say. The first two who arrived were armed. I was then beaten, and I could no longer tell whether the other men were armed too.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you lose consciousness as a result of the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you regain consciousness there at your farm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. There's a fountain there. I washed up -- I regained consciousness. They poured water on me, and then I regained consciousness.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you questioned at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, I was. They asked why I had taken my wife and children away to Serbia, and why I was there, why I had returned.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Other than that, can you recall the topics of any other questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: They asked about weapons, whether I had any weapons stashed away, and to tell them where. I told them I didn't have anything except for the rifle that I had hidden. It was a licensed hunting rifle that I had from before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: As a result of you telling them about the rifle, did they search for it or find it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: No, they didn't search for it. I had the impression that they'd found it already. And they didn't tell me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you retained in any way, tied up in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. They handcuffed me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And were you taken somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as they tied us up, they took us to a place called Rovasi.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that in just a moment. Was anything taken from your premises, from your farm or your property?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, they used a horse that was there to take away some food, some corn, some flour. They took some of these things and took it to a village nearby. But where to exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours would just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Don't mention the name of your home village, don't mention it, but how far is Rovasi from it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, because I can't be accurate about this, I think it must be about 5 or 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you walk there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And there, were you incarcerated in a building that was known to people as a stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the villagers of Rovasi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And can you tell us the ethnicity of the men who captured you, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the five men? Is there -- can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: They were Muslims too, because they had the insignia that I told you about, which stood for their army. I didn't know these people.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened to you when you arrived in Rovasi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: When I arrived in Rovasi, I sat down on a tree trunk. They brought me some food, and took me away to this stable. The stable was about 400 or 500 metres from the mosque in Rovasi.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you remain in that stable once you were placed inside it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: We remained in the stable -- you mean until we were transferred to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That's exactly right. How long did you stay there altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, we were, that means myself, Jokic and the other people, we were there until 1993. That was after the 7th, but I can't remember the date. It was sometime after the 7th of January, but I can't give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. So depending on the precise month or date of your capture, you were there at least for a matter of many months, several months.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. When you first entered the stable, did you see any other people inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Can I name these people?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, what I'd like you to do is tell the Trial Chamber, if you know these details, the names of these people, the ethnicity of these people, and where they came from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Okay. There were four persons. The first one I met was Osman, his first name was Osman. The second person, and I don't know his last name, his first name was Kasim. The third name, again, I didn't know his last name, the first name was Suljo. The fourth name was Jakov Dzokic. These were the four persons.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: All right. Tell the Trial Chamber -- well, let me withdraw that. Did you spend many weeks and months in company with these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I was with Jakov Dzokic all the time. And as for the remaining three persons, Osman, Suljo, and Kasim, I really can't say whether we spent a month and a half or two months together, but they weren't there for that long. I don't know when they arrived. They arrived before I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. We'll talk about Jakov Dzokic later, but let's concentrate on the three men you've told us were named Osman, Kasim, and Suljo. What ethnicity were those men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know, or were you ever informed by them, as to why they were in that stable there along with you and Jakov?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I can tell you what I was told by Osman. Osman told me that he had arrived in this stable, in this prison, because he had slaughtered some cattle, some lambs, and given it to the Serb army, whereas Kasim and the other man ended up there because, purportedly, they had taken weapons from their people and given it to our army.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they tell you where they were from, these three Muslim men, Osman, Suljo, and Kasim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They said that all three of them were from Kamenica, in Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did the three men you've told us, who eventually left the stable, did they all depart on the one occasion, or did they go separately? Or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I think that they all left together, but I'm not entirely sure. I suppose they left together.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's turn to Mr. Jakov Dzokic. What ethnicity was he, and where was he from, if you were told?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Jakov Dzokic was a Serb by ethnicity, born in Kalabace, which is in Sekovici municipality. That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was he a young man or middle-aged man or older man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: He was a young man. He was 18 or 20, just out of the army, the JNA, as it existed then. At least that's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. And did he explain to you or tell you how he came to find himself there in that stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, he did explain. He was on his way from Ilijasi, which is near Sarajevo, where he had been serving his military service, so he was on his way home. He got into a car. He hitchhiked a ride and got into a car with someone. And instead of getting out in Vlasenica and turn left to Sekovici, he went to Konjevic Polje, because the people were on their way to Bratunac and he didn't know that. He got out in Konjevic Polje. There was some two or three men there who interrogated him, who he was and where he was from. He said that he jumped into the other river, crossed the river, and continued on to Rovasi.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. And did he come to tell you or explain to you how that led to his actually being held there inside the stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, this is what he told me: That he was on his way to Rovasi. There's a road there, and he moved on that road. And he came across two men in uniform who stopped him and asked for his IDs. When they found his IDs - he had his military ID on him, or something like that - they told him that they would arrest him and that he would be arrested by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did he explain to you that's what, in fact, happened and that's how he found himself in the stable, having -- because he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: This is what he told me. And then he came to the stable. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he explain -- sorry, did you see how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: He had a uniform, a partial uniform, whereas the other part of his clothing was not military. This is what he wore when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. I want you now to turn your attention to the inside of the stable, and describe the conditions to the Trial Chamber. Briefly, we don't need to go into a huge amount of detail, but briefly tell the Trial Chamber what was on the floor, what you used for a lavatory, the bedding that was in there, if any, and the food.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: The conditions were uncomfortable. Everything was dirty; that goes without saying. We used a bucket to relieve ourselves; it was inside, indoors. The food was bad, naturally. The food was brought in on a daily basis, once or twice a day. Sometimes they wouldn't bring anything in a day. The stable did not have a proper floor. I think there was just a concrete floor and then hay strewn on it. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In the time that you were in the stable, did you start to develop a problem with lice, lice infestation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did the other inmates also suffer from the same problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: They did. They had it too. All of us had lice.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you ever beaten whilst in the stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: While I was in the stable, an older man used to come. He came twice and beat me. And there was also a younger man who used to come, accompanied by another man, and I heard that allegedly he was in the police somewhere. I don't know whether this is true or not. So they used to come and beat me as well.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were there guards at the stable guarding you and the inmates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, some had partial uniforms or some other clothing on them, a combination of the two.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've told us that you were there for many months. In that period of time, did you see or hear anything that gives you a clue as to what the occupation of the guards was? Were they farmers or butchers, policemen, soldiers? Can you tell the Trial Chamber if, in all of the time that you were there, you managed to get into -- any insight into what their occupation was. Now, I'm talking about the guards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I couldn't really say what their occupation was. I couldn't say. They served as guards there. They would rotate. I don't know their names either. I just remember the name of one of them, but not of the others.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said that you were beaten, and you've described two men who beat you. Was it just confined to those two men, or were you beaten by other men, other than the two that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I described them because they would beat us more often. However, there were groups that would beat us, and there were groups that wouldn't beat us, that the guards wouldn't let inside.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did the guards themselves ever beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I don't remember the guards beating us.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And, while we're on this topic, you've told us about you were receiving beatings. What about your fellow inmates? Were they subjected to the same treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, they were beaten as well. So they beat the two of us, and the three Muslims that were there, they got beaten too.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've earlier mentioned that the three Muslim men eventually left, and you're not entirely sure if they all left at the same time or precisely how long they were in there before they left. What I want to ask you is this: Can you recall how it was that they came to be released, if that was associated with any event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. A delegation had arrived from Kamenica, at least that's what they told us. And they took them and -- took them away. I think that they left together, but I might have forgotten the details.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, can you offer any assistance with the identity of this delegation from Kamenica? Did you see them, did you speak to them, or did you hear anything about them that could tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you who they were, what their names were. They didn't say that to me. They simply said, or rather, I heard that they were from some kind of a command in Kamenica and that they took these people to Kamenica. Now, what their names were, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Well, that's what I want to know about. Who told you about them being from a command? And what sort of understanding did you have of that, this command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, the command was probably some kind of a command located in Kamenica. I don't know any other details. They simply told us that when they came to pick up the three men. They said that they would go to Kamenica, and Kasim said that these people were from the command, some people from the command, and that they came there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you actually lay eyes on the delegation? Did you actually see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, I saw them. There were a couple of people in that group. I couldn't describe their appearance to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Okay. If you can't describe their appearance, can you tell us if they were dressed as soldiers? Did they have any uniforms on, and were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I think that they wore civilian clothing. They were not armed. As far as I could tell, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a gentleman named Branko Sekulic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in the stable that you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. He came to the stable; he was brought there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you recall when he was brought there? If you can't recall the -- you may not be able to tell us the date; I doubt that. Could you tell us the season, at least, or the month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I think that it was in summertime. I couldn't tell you the month or the date. But summertime.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Incidentally, during -- throughout this period of your incarceration in the stable, and indeed later in Srebrenica, did you ever have access to a calendar, or did people inform you as to what the dates were, what month you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: By the time Branko Sekulic arrived, had you lost track of the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is that -- I'm sorry, do I take your answer to be that you had lost track of the date, you didn't know what month or what date it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I didn't know what month it was, let alone date. How would I know that? It was summertime, but I couldn't tell you more than that. I don't remember days, dates, months.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Sekulic, did you know him prior to his arrival in the stable, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you recall the first time he was brought into the prison? Into the stable, I should say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, I do recall certain things. I don't recall some other things.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How was he brought into the stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: They brought him in. There were several men who led him and threw him into the stable. I remember that he was wounded, that he couldn't stand on one leg, he couldn't put his weight on one leg. They beat him as they threw him into the stable.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, I don't think it's in dispute that you ended up spending many, many months with this man. In the time following his arrival in the stable, did you hear his story, how he came to be captured, where he was from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He told us that he hailed from Milici Brdo. He gave us his first name, his last name, said that he had been captured. I just remember that he told me that he had been captured in a place called -- I can't remember, but definitely at the front line, somewhere there. That's what he told us, that he had been captured there. And then he spent several days in another place, which I've forgotten in the meantime, the name of that other place. And then from there he was taken to the stable where I was.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'd like to know specifically is this: Did he ever say to you or make clear to you that he was a soldier, that he had been captured in fighting and then placed into custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: This is what he told me: He said that he had come to visit his father, and that he was at the front line. I don't know the details, but most likely he was in the army at the front line. And this is where he was captured, wounded and captured, and taken to the prison in Cerska, to the stable.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. And just so that we can keep some idea of time, if possible, can you tell us if he arrived while the three Muslim men were still there or whether he arrived after they'd left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: They had left. I think that they had left. I don't remember exactly, but I think that they had left.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a man named Dragan Ilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was he in the stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. He came later.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do I take it from that that he arrived before or after Jakov Dzokic, or you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I can't be sure a hundred per cent, but I think that he came after Sekulic. Jakov and I were there, but I am not entirely sure. At any rate, he arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And how old was this Dragan Ilic when he was taken into the stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: He was a young man, 18, 20 years. He was young.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you hear his story from him as to how it was that he was captured, and where he was from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, he told me about that. He said that he had been in Kasaba, in a place called Kasaba, which is near his place, and that he had been captured in Kasaba, or rather, that some friends of his captured him. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us about the three Muslim men, you've told us about Mr. Dzokic, you've told us about Dragan Ilic. Were there any other men who were placed into the stables along with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: There was Sekulic there, Jakov Dzokic, Dragan Ilic. And later on another man came in called Dusan Cestic. He was also brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were there any Gypsies in the stable with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now I remember. There was a Gypsy from Kasaba who allegedly had been captured for looting some stores, stealing from the stores and taking the goods away. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know -- I'm not quite sure how to frame this, but do you know the ethnicity of the Gypsy, if he apparently had some overlay to his Gypsy background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: No, I don't know. The people who knew him said that he was a Gypsy from Kasaba. I don't know any other details about his background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can go -- you can lead the witness on this, if it's important for you. If not, I suggest you move to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The other man that you've mentioned, Dusan Cestic, what ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: He was a Serb from Korijan. I knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How long was Dusan Cestic in the stable with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Not long. I can't remember now how many days, but not long. He died there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In the stable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You've mentioned earlier in your testimony that beatings that you suffered, and that the other inmates suffered, was in any let-up in the beatings that you were -- that you suffered? In other words, did the beatings continue when these men were also in the stable, Cestic, the Gypsy man, Branko Sekulic, Jakov Dokic, Dragan Ilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Well, there were people who would come and beat us, but there were also days when no one would beat us in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. The man Cestic, do you know how it was that he died? Was it as a result of a beating or some other -- some other cause?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I don't know. I only remember that before that, the first or the second day after he arrived, he said, should any of us survive, we should all say that he was ill, that he had pain in his kidneys, and that we should tell his children afterwards that he had died in prison.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Gypsy man, did he stay in the prison from the time of his arrival until the time of your departure, or was he released at some earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: He was released too. I'm not sure when, but he was released too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, because there's one thing, sort of, which hasn't been followed up. This man Cestic, Dusan Cestic, who you said died in prison but you couldn't say as a result of -- whether it was a result of a beating or not, and you also told us that he had kidney problems, according to what he told you himself. Was he ever beaten, this Cestic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was beaten too, of course. He complained about being ill, though. That's what he told me. His kidneys hurt. He said he would not make it. He was in a very poor condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on this topic for too long, but I want you to tell the Trial Chamber of the intensity of the beatings that you're talking about. Tell the Trial Chamber whether instruments were used, first of all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I'll tell you one thing I remember quite clearly: There were two men who came. I didn't know their names. They carried a piece of wood or a stick. One held my hand and the other beat me with that long piece of wood. I remember that clearly. As for the other instruments that were used to beat me, I really don't remember. I was beaten so badly that I couldn't even think straight. One of them came, and I heard that he was from Skugrici. He was an elderly man; he may have been around 60. He also came and he punched me with his fist. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you kicked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: This particular man from Skugrici used his fist, and the other one used the wooden stick. And they kicked me to, those two other men who came. I'm not sure about their names.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was there blood visible in the stable? Now, I mean on the walls or on the floor or on the clothing of the inmates or on their faces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, there was, on our faces, on our clothes. The other people too were being -- had been beaten. When I entered, I realised immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Was a woman ever brought into the stables?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, and you can proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, you've told us of conditions in this stable and some of the unpleasant things that happened. Were there also, from time to time, acts of kindness extended towards you by people of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were acts of kindness. I will mention some things that I remember, although I must have forgotten a lot. I do remember one particular person; I think his first name was Salko, a man Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from Cerska. I'm not sure about the hamlet. He would come over and bring us fruit to eat, pears, apples, plums, all sorts of things. He would bring food, bread, soup, and meat once, even meat. I remember that. I thanked this man, and if I ran into him today, if he's still alive and well, I would love to really congratulate him on everything that he did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the acts of kindness of Salko, was there a man named Muradif who occasionally brought you -- or who did bring you, on one occasion at least, some soap and a razor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes, it's good of you to remind me of that. This is another man who, on a number of occasions, brought us food -- actually, I think he was in charge of that prison for a while. He would bring us food. And I remember that once he brought a shaving kit and some soap, as well as water. We had water inside, but he brought some nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. And while we're on this topic, one last question: Did a neighbour of yours, and I don't want you to mention his name, but did a neighbour of yours from your village, your area, also come on one occasion, or at least one occasion, and also bring food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was another man, a Muslim man, from my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest that we go into private session and we get the name of this person now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I apologise for having left my microphone on. I think I've been fairly good up until now. Yes, can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that you're moving to another topic, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if it's convenient for you, I think we can stop here. We'll have a 25-minute break, and resume soon after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the end of your stay in the stable. You've already mentioned that you moved to Srebrenica. Can you recall approximately when you moved from the stable to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: That was in 1993, in January. I don't know the date. I know that it was after the 7th of January, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did men come to your cell? To the stable, I should say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: I don't remember if they were armed or not, if they carried a pistol or not. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Now, when they first arrived at the stable, did they tell you the reason why you were being taken, moved out of the stable and taken to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. They said that we would be on our way to Srebrenica, where we were to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you then set about your journey off to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Yes. We left the stable and headed towards a hamlet in Cerska, where the elementary school was. There was -- that was where we left the vehicle, the tractor that we were driving on, and we continued on towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to establish who is "we". Who was in the party at that stage? And I'm talking about not the soldiers -- sorry, the men who came to collect you, but rather the inmates. Was it just yourself, or was it other inmates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: Sekulic Branko, Jakov Dzokic, myself, Dragan Ilic, and Andja, whose last name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. And you travelled, as you said, on a tractor, and you were taken to a small village and into the -- and to the elementary school. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if anything happened at the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C007
utterances.text: When we reached the elementary school, I don't think the building was destroyed. There were lots of locals around. They watched us but didn't touch us. We got onto this tractor, or cart, rather, those who could, who were able to, and they drove us on to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What do you mean by that phrase, "those of us who were able to"?
